purpose: Adds a two-tier (command vs interactive) rate-limiting system to the Probot app — per-repo hourly, per-user daily, per-PR cooldown, and a shared daily token budget — persisted in a new rate_limits table across SQLite/Postgres/MySQL and the JSON fallback, with reserve-at-check-time accounting, gated /rate-limits and /rate-limits-reset admin commands, and clamped RATE_LIMIT_* env overrides.
riskRationale: Well-structured, fully parameterized, and unusually well-tested (mock-store unit suite plus a real SQLite-backed end-to-end suite). No critical or security defects found: the per-PR cooldown is correctly repo-scoped, the admin gate is case-insensitive with a safe empty default, denial comments are upserted via a stable marker, and reservations shrink the check-then-run race from minutes to milliseconds. The remaining risk is robustness rather than defects: check-then-reserve is still not atomic so a burst of concurrent webhooks can overshoot every cap; the store facade fails open so the guardrail silently disappears when the DB is unavailable; the daily token budget is charged from fixed tier estimates (only the review path reconciles real usage); a slash command in a threaded reply double-fires two subscribers; and rate limiting defaults ON so existing installs are throttled immediately, including auto-triggered reviews.
breakingChanges: Rate limiting defaults to enabled:true — existing deployments immediately throttle slash commands, @mention conversations, replies, and auto-reviews (10/hr per repo, 50/day per user, 500k tokens/day) and will start seeing 'Rate Limit Reached' comments
New rate_limits table plus four indexes auto-migrate into the learning-store schema on next startup (idempotent; JSON fallback initializes an empty rate_limits array)
New /rate-limits and /rate-limits-reset admin commands gated behind rateLimiting.adminUsers (empty by default, so inert until configured)
New RATE_LIMIT_* env overrides; AgentConfig now requires the rateLimiting field (buildConfig() and DEFAULT_CONFIG supply defaults)
pr.opened/pr.synchronize auto-reviews now consume the command-tier hourly and per-user daily quota, so a busy repo or frequent pusher can silently stop auto-reviewing

text: A comprehensive, well-engineered rate-limiting feature: a clean single-source-of-truth RateLimiter core over a minimal RateLimitStore contract, a thin app-side helper that reserves capacity at check time and reconciles actuals after the run, fully parameterized SQL consistent across all backends, schema-validated env config with bounds clamping, gated admin commands, and genuinely strong test coverage including a real SQLite-backed end-to-end suite. Earlier review iterations already fixed the cross-repo cooldown bug, the global-reset fallthrough, and the unbounded 429 comment path; what remains before merge is the residual non-atomic check-then-reserve race, the fail-open store path, estimate-only token accounting, the threaded-reply double-fire, and several config/admin footguns.

reasoning: The feature is sound, well-tested, and materially improved over earlier iterations, but two important findings directly weaken the PR's stated purpose of preventing cost runaway: the non-atomic check-then-reserve lets a burst of concurrent webhooks overshoot every cap, and the store fails open so enforcement silently disappears on a DB outage. Both require interface-level changes (a transactional/atomic reserve in the store, and threading real token usage through all subscribers) that are not safe one-click automated fixes, and the auto-triggered 429-comment and threaded-reply double-fire behaviors should be closed before shipping.

message: The reserve-at-check-time design is the right call: checkReview() inserts a rate_limits row charged at the tier estimate the moment all checks pass, so in-flight (minutes-long) LLM runs count against cooldowns, per-repo/user caps, and the token budget before they finish, and recordReview() reconciles the row with actual usage afterward — closing the dominant check-then-run race. Failed runs keep their reservation, so attempts still count.

All new rate-limit SQL is fully parameterized (no injection surface), the cooldown lookup is correctly scoped by (repo, pr_number, tier) — fixing the cross-repo collision a naive pr-number-only key would cause — timestamps are ISO-8601 UTC consistently with the JSON fallback so comparisons are chronological across backends, and the migration ships indexes that match the actual query patterns.

Test coverage goes beyond pure mocks: a comprehensive mock-store unit suite exercises every limit, cooldown expiry, per-repo scoping, reset, cleanup, disabled mode, and 429 formatting, plus a separate end-to-end suite drives the real SQLite-backed LearningStore (record, count, token sums, last-time scoping, aggregation, reset, cleanup, reservation reconciliation) — giving high confidence both enforcement backends agree.

Admin commands are correctly gated behind rateLimiting.adminUsers with a case-insensitive comparison (GitHub usernames are case-insensitive) and a safe empty-by-default allow-list, resets use parameterized deletes, and the space-separated --repo/--user form is explicitly rejected as invalid syntax instead of silently falling through to a global reset.
All RATE_LIMIT_* env overrides are clamped into sane bounds, so hostile or malformed values (negative, absurdly large, non-numeric) cannot silently disable rate limiting or set an infinite budget.

Deferring @mention replies to ConversationSubscriber avoids both a double LLM call and a double rate-limit charge for the same comment — a real correctness improvement that also keeps the interactive-tier cooldown shared on the same PR.

Denial notices are upserted via postOrUpdateComment with a stable '<!-- rate-limit-reached -->' marker, so repeated blocked attempts update a single comment instead of accumulating API-spam, and the denial path is wrapped so a failed comment post cannot crash the subscriber.

checkReview() performs four independent awaits (repo count, user count, last-PR-time, token sum) and only then inserts the reservation row (line 183) — none of it inside a transaction. The reservation narrows the check-then-run race from minutes to milliseconds, but because the EventBus executes subscribers concurrently (SUBSCRIBER_CONCURRENCY=10) and GitHub delivers webhooks in parallel, a burst of simultaneous /review or @mention events can all read under-limit counts before any reservation commits and collectively overshoot reviewsPerRepoPerHour, reviewsPerUserPerDay, the per-PR cooldown, and the daily token budget by up to the concurrency factor — the exact cost-runaway scenario this PR exists to prevent.
suggestion: Make the count checks and the reservation insert a single atomic operation: wrap them in one SQL transaction (SqlAdapter already exposes transaction(); better-sqlite3 serializes writes) or use a conditional INSERT ... SELECT that re-checks the count in SQL, so concurrent requests observe each other's reservations before any run starts. For the JSON backend, add a per-process mutex around check+reserve. At minimum, document that limits are approximate under bursts.

message: The LearningStore facade fails open on every rate-limit read: countRateLimitActions() returns 0, sumRateLimitTokens() returns 0, and getLastRateLimitTime() returns null on error, and checkReview() also logs-and-continues if the reservation insert throws (rate-limiter.ts:191-194). Whenever the store is unavailable (connection failure, SQLite lock, JSON parse error), every limit silently passes and no usage is recorded — the cost-control guardrail disappears precisely when there may be an infrastructure problem. This matches the codebase's graceful-degradation convention, but for a cost-control mechanism failing open is the wrong default.
suggestion: Fail closed on the rate-limit read paths (deny when usage cannot be measured — e.g. return the configured limit or a denial result), or pair the store with a short-lived in-memory cache of last-known counts so limits do not vanish on a transient outage. At minimum, make this a deliberate, documented, configurable trade-off with loud error-level logging and a metric/alert.

message: recordRateLimit() accepts tokensUsed, but only ReviewSubscriber passes actual usage (review.ts:88 via result.usage?.totalTokens); the other seven subscribers (fix, audit, analyze, auto-analyze, explain, discover, conversation, reply) all charge the fixed tier estimate (25k command / 5k interactive). A single large review or fix run can spend several times its 25k estimate, so real daily spend can far exceed the advertised 500k token budget without ever tripping the limiter — the budget behaves as an action-count proxy rather than a token cap, undercutting the PR's cost-control goal.
suggestion: Thread actual token usage from each handler's run result into recordRateLimit (the handlers already expose usage in their return values), falling back to the tier estimate only when actuals are unavailable, and consider reserving at max(estimate, recent actual) so consistently underestimated runs cannot silently blow the budget.

message: ReplySubscriber only defers for /dismiss and @mentions, but every command subscriber also subscribes to review_comment.created. A threaded reply whose body is a slash command such as /fix, /analyze, or /review therefore triggers BOTH ReplySubscriber (interactive tier) and the matching command subscriber — two LLM calls and two rate-limit charges (one command-tier, one interactive-tier) from a single user message. The dual-fire predates this PR, but the new reservation/record logic now doubles the charge against the per-user daily and token budgets, directly contradicting the cost-control goal.
suggestion: Mirror the /dismiss guard: when parseCommand(body) returns any known slash command, skip the conversational reply so the dedicated command subscriber owns the event and one user message produces one LLM run and one rate-limit record.

message: Auto-triggered events do not suppress the denial comment. FixSubscriber (issue.labeled with autofix-trigger) and AutoAnalyzeSubscriber (issue.opened with needs-analysis) call checkRateLimit without postDenialComment: false, so a rate-limit denial posts a public 'Rate Limit Reached' comment on an issue/PR where no user invoked the bot. This is inconsistent with ReviewSubscriber (review.ts:59-62), which deliberately enforces limits silently for auto-triggered pr.opened/pr.synchronize events.
suggestion: Mirror the ReviewSubscriber pattern: compute isCommandInvoked from the event type and pass postDenialComment: isCommandInvoked (or false) in fix.ts and auto-analyze.ts so auto-triggered denials stay silent.

message: Auto-triggered pr.opened/pr.synchronize reviews are routed through the SAME command-tier guards as user slash commands, sharing the per-repo hourly budget (10/hr) and charging the per-user daily quota to the PR author/pusher via extractActor. Two consequences: (1) on an active repo, push-driven re-reviews silently consume the hourly budget and can block legitimate /review or /fix commands (and vice versa); (2) re-review-on-push now silently no-ops for any push arriving within the 2-minute prCooldownMinutes window — a behavior regression from before this PR where every push triggered a re-review.
suggestion: Decide deliberately whether auto-reviews are in scope: either separate their accounting from user commands (a distinct action/tier or config flag so they cannot starve each other) or exclude auto-triggered events from the per-user daily limit while keeping the repo-hourly cap, and log at info level when an auto-review is skipped due to rate limiting so the silent stops are visible.

message: A bare /rate-limits-reset with no flags (or unknown flags) falls through to resetAll(), wiping every rate-limit record across ALL repos and users in the shared store; combining --all with --repo/--user silently lets --all win, and combining --repo with --user drops the user filter. A mistyped or syntax-checking command can therefore destroy far more than intended, and reset semantics also diverge between backends (the SQL adapter deletes by repo only when both are supplied while the JSON store applies an OR filter — sql-adapter.ts:1066 vs json-db.ts:1172).
suggestion: Require an explicit, mutually exclusive scope: reject a flag-less reset (or default it to the current PR's repo) with a usage message, reserve resetAll() for an explicit --all, reject combinations of --all with --repo/--user, and align the JSON and SQL reset predicates for the both-arguments case.

message: recordRateLimit() is only called inside the `if (result)` branch, so when handlePRReview returns null (a legitimate skip such as nothing to review — not an exception), the reservation row is never reconciled and stays charged the full 25k-token estimate while also pinning the per-PR cooldown. Repeated no-op /review invocations can therefore drain the daily token budget with zero LLM spend and leave users with confusing cooldown denials for reviews that never ran.
suggestion: Reconcile the reservation even on a null result (e.g. recordRateLimit(..., reservation, 0)), reserving the full estimate only for genuine failures/throws, so only real LLM work consumes the budget.

message: Setting any numeric limit to 0 via env override (e.g. RATE_LIMIT_REVIEWS_PER_REPO_HOUR=0, RATE_LIMIT_REVIEWS_PER_USER_DAY=0, RATE_LIMIT_DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET=0 — clampInt's minimum is 0, and negative values clamp to 0) makes the count >= 0 comparison always true, so every action is silently denied with a 429 comment and the bot appears broken. An operator who sets 0 expecting 'off' effectively shuts the bot down; only enabled=false actually disables enforcement.
suggestion: Clamp count/token limits to a minimum of 1 (or document that 0 intentionally denies everything and validate estimates >= 1), and point operators to enabled: false as the supported way to turn limiting off.

message: The migration runs DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_rate_limits_pr_tier on EVERY startup. That index never existed in any released schema (dev scaffolding left in), and the statement is MySQL-incompatible — MySQL does not support IF EXISTS on DROP INDEX and requires DROP INDEX ... ON <table> — so applyMigrations() can throw on a mysql:// deployment (which already cannot run the pre-existing CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS statements).
suggestion: Remove the DROP INDEX line entirely (the idx_rate_limits_repo_pr_tier index is created by the CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS line) and, if MySQL/Postgres are in scope, translate the dialect-specific statements so the migration block runs on every backend.

message: The reported headroom is imprecise and can be malformed: budgetHeadroomActions divides by estimatedTokens (0 yields Infinity, and Math.floor(0/0) yields NaN when the estimate and budget are both 0), remaining is computed from pre-reservation counts (ignoring this request's own reservation), and resetAt always reports end-of-day while the repo-hourly cap resets hourly. Admin/status consumers and the 429 message can therefore show stale, missing, or non-finite numbers.
suggestion: Guard the division (e.g. estimate > 0 ? Math.floor(Math.max(0, budget - used) / estimate) : Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), subtract this request's reservation from remaining, and return a resetAt reflecting the soonest bound (min of hourly and daily reset) or document these as best-effort.

message: Unauthorized users who run /rate-limits or /rate-limits-reset are silently ignored with no response at all. Combined with the empty default for adminUsers, an operator who forgets to configure RATE_LIMIT_ADMIN_USERS gets a silent no-op with no discoverable feedback that the command exists or was blocked, making the admin feature effectively invisible.
suggestion: Post a short 'not authorized' notice for recognized rate-limit commands from non-admins, or log the attempt at warn level so operators can detect and configure admin access.

message: rateLimiter.cleanup() runs once at startup only; a long-lived process never prunes rows older than retention (48h default), so the rate_limits table grows unbounded (~1000+ rows/day on a busy app) until the next restart, inflating every count/sum query. This is a scalability/maintainability concern rather than a correctness one.
suggestion: Also prune during record (e.g. opportunistically delete rows older than retention inside recordRateLimitAction) or schedule periodic cleanup (setInterval) alongside the startup pass, clearing the timer on shutdown.

message: recordRateLimitAction() pushes a row and calls save(), which serializes the entire JSON database to disk on every rate-limited action; under sustained command traffic the JSON fallback rewrites the whole file per action. The debounced save coalesces bursts, but the synchronous flush on each reserved action still defeats the debounce.
suggestion: Debounce/batch saves (mark dirty and flush once per event-loop tick or at exit), or accept the cost since the JSON backend is a documented degraded fallback.

message: The getStatus aggregation SELECT github_user as user, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY github_user returns a row with user:null when github_user is NULL, but the declared return type is { user: string; count: number }. The rate_limits schema allows NULL github_user, so a manual/malformed row would surface as the string 'null' in /rate-limits output and violate the type contract.
suggestion: Add a WHERE github_user IS NOT NULL clause (or COALESCE(github_user, 'unknown')) and a NOT NULL guard, keeping the query aligned with the typed return.

message: A denial comment is posted/upserted on every denied event. Under a burst of blocked attempts (e.g. cooldown spam), each denial triggers a paginated comment fetch (up to 5 pages) plus a PATCH, and 429 notices get interleaved into active conversation threads — extra GitHub API load and noisy UX.
suggestion: Gate comment posting on whether the same marker was already posted recently (e.g. only post once per PR per limit window), or notify only on the first denial within a reset window.

message: extractActor falls back to 'unknown' when no comment author/sender/PR author is derivable. All such actions share one 'unknown' bucket in the per-user daily limit and count toward the shared token budget, so a set of events without identifiable actors can spuriously block unrelated actions or consume budget without attribution.
suggestion: Log a warning when the actor resolves to 'unknown' so un-attributable usage is visible, and consider excluding or treating 'unknown' separately in the per-user daily aggregation.
